The evaluation is limited to simulated environments and does not include real robot transfer. Our compute budget (${\sim}80$ GPU hours on a single GPU) restricts the scale of the factorial design; larger sweeps may reveal additional interaction effects. Seed counts of four to five per condition provide sufficient power for binary CIVO classification but may not capture fine-grained effect sizes across all environmental conditions.

\paragraph{Environment Complexity Dependence.} CIVO onset exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with environment complexity. Across six DeepMind Control Suite tasks spanning 1 to 21 degrees of freedom (DoF), CIVO occurs exclusively in 6-DoF environments: Walker Walk (3/5 seeds, 60\%) and Cheetah Run (3/4 seeds, 75\%). Lower-DoF environments do not trigger the phenomenon. In Cartpole Swingup (1 DoF), the gate degrades performance through non-value-driven mechanisms (NVE $< 0.1\times$); the single-joint dynamics appear too simple for value overestimation to cascade through learned temporal embeddings. In Hopper Hop (4 DoF), the gate causes transient learning delay followed by recovery to 85\% of baseline performance after extended training (168K steps vs.\ the standard 105K evaluation window), though this observation rests on a single seed ($n{=}1$) and warrants replication. At higher DoF, a different obstacle emerges. Both Quadruped Walk (12 DoF) and Humanoid Walk (21 DoF) baselines exhibit intrinsic value overestimation (NVE $= 4.7\times$ and $12.97\times$, respectively) without any gate mechanism. These failures stem from known scaling challenges of DreamerV3 in high-dimensional action spaces~\citep{hafner2025dreamerv3} and preclude clean isolation of gate-induced CIVO from pre-existing overestimation. Our empirical characterization of CIVO is therefore grounded in 6-DoF moderate-complexity locomotion, and whether the onset boundary extends to higher DoF remains contingent on achieving stable baselines in those regimes.
